newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers to discuss beef label compromise.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers to discuss beef label compromise.

text.p: European Union farm ministers were to discuss on Monday a compromise on compulsory beef labelling after unanimously rejecting a proposal that would give the European Parliament a joint say, EU officials said.
The compromise, drafted by the Dutch EU Presidency, would give the parliament only a consultative role, but would still make it obligatory to state the origin of the beef.

The European Commission's joint proposal on identification of cattle and beef labelling, aimed at restoring consumer confidence after the mad cow disease health scare, would oblige member countries to label beef from January 2000.
"No one supported the European Commission," a Commission spokesman said, referring to its bid to give the European Parliament more power over EU decision-making.
Italy, noting virtual agreement on identification but divisions over labelling, wanted to split the proposal but this was opposed by the Commission.
A majority, led by France and Germany, were in favour of compulsory beef labelling but others, notably Britain and Ireland, had strong objections.
"I am in favour, very much in favour and even more so in favour," French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur told Reuters before the meeting, adding he hoped that agreement would rapidly be reached.

Portuguese Farm Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva, another supporter of compulsory labelling, said the proposal must be changed but it would need unanimous agreement among the 15 member states to overrule the Commission.
Danish Farm Minister Henrik Dam Kristensen said he did not think agreement would be reached.
"I'm a little bit pessimistic," he told reporters before the meeting. "I think the proposal is too bureaucratic."
British officials said Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg would ask for more time to study the revised proposal, presented earlier this month, as there were points he didn't like.
Britain believes that the proposal would stir nationalist sentiment and create a barrier to trade in the EU single market.
